insider_note: The add-and-subtract-1 trick works for any rational function whose numerator and denominator have the same degree — always look for it before trying a harder substitution.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Split into a proper fraction
steps.margin_note: First mark. x²/(1+x²) = 1 − 1/(1+x²) — always rewrite an improper fraction this way before integrating.
steps.memory_tip: Numerator degree equals denominator degree ⇒ subtract 1 to make the fraction proper.
steps.why: Adding and subtracting 1 in the numerator rewrites x² as (1+x²)−1, splitting the improper fraction into a constant 1 minus the standard form 1/(1+x²), which integrates directly.
common_mistakes: Trying to integrate x²/(1+x²) as it stands, without first adding and subtracting 1 in the numerator.
Losing the minus sign in front of 1/(1+x²).

steps.label: Integrate and apply the limits
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Tan⁻¹1 = π/4 is a standard value — memorise it alongside Tan⁻¹0 = 0.
steps.memory_tip: x − Tan⁻¹x is the antiderivative to remember whenever x²/(1+x²) appears.
steps.why: ∫dx = x and ∫dx/(1+x²) = Tan⁻¹x, so the antiderivative is x − Tan⁻¹x; substituting x=1 gives Tan⁻¹1 = π/4 and x=0 gives Tan⁻¹0 = 0.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that Tan⁻¹1 = π/4, not π/2.
Dropping the −Tan⁻¹0 term even though it equals 0.
